extracted.intended_audience: educated British public, Parliamentarians, and readers concerned with constitutional government and public administration
extracted.subtask_description: A sustained eighteenth‑century political essay arguing standards for good administration, the proper relation of executive and legislature, and the public character required of ministers in a free constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration must be placed in trustworthy hands
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing can render [the selection of administrators] a point of indifference to the nation; the executory system must not be disposed of agreeable to the uncontrolled pleasure of any one man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay insists that leaving the whole executory system to the uncontrolled pleasure of a single person, however virtuous, is 'a plan of polity defective' and 'consequentially erroneous in every part of it.' Administration must inspire public trust and be selected on grounds beyond private will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration ought to correspond to the legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: Every sort of government ought to have its administration correspondent to its legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If administration is not correspondent to the legislature, things fall into 'hideous disorder.' In a free commonwealth laws (result of general consent) require an executory system composed of persons the people can depend on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary control through refusal of support
rubrics_metrics.description: It had always been held the first duty of Parliament 'to refuse to support government, until power was in the hands of persons who were acceptable to the people, or while factions predominated...in which the nation had no confidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The power of Parliamentary refusal served historically as the people's negative control over appointments; losing this check undermines both Parliament and popular confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular election (or its constitutional equivalent) is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: The popular election of magistrates, and popular disposition of rewards and honors, is one of the first advantages of a free state... Without it, or something equivalent to it, perhaps the people cannot long enjoy the substance of freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the exact form of election differs, the effects of popular selection (accountability, public confidence) must be secured by the constitution to maintain freedom and the 'vivifying energy of good government.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions must have preventive operation to exclude bad men
rubrics_metrics.description: Every good political institution must have a preventive operation as well as a remedial. It ought to have a natural tendency to exclude bad men from government, and not to trust for the safety of the state to subsequent punishment alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying only on punishment (tardy and uncertain) is inadequate; constitutions should be designed to prevent unfit persons from obtaining power in the first place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public officeholders should have prior public esteem
rubrics_metrics.description: Before men are put forward into the great trusts of the state, they ought by their conduct to have obtained such a degree of estimation in their country, as may be some sort of pledge and security to the public, that they will not abuse those trusts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A record of affection, good opinion, and confidence of fellow-citizens is a meaningful security against abuse of power; appointments should favor those with proven public regard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid appointing those with no social or public connections
rubrics_metrics.description: That man who before he comes into power has no friends, or who coming into power is obliged to desert his friends...is a person who ought never to be suffered...to continue in any of those situations which confer the lead and direction of all our public affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officials whose importance begins and ends with their office, lacking ties to landed or commercial interests or public sympathy, lack necessary 'connection with the interest of the people.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude cabals and knots without public principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Those knots or cabals of men who have got together, avowedly without any public principle...ought never to be suffered to domineer in the state; because they have no connection with the sentiments and opinions of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political groupings formed merely for private advantage and lacking public principles are widely odious and unsuitable to govern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government should aim for a practicable degree of popular content
rubrics_metrics.description: The controversy is about that degree of good humor in the people, which may possibly be attained, and ought certainly to be looked for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute unanimity is impossible; prudent statesmanship seeks a reasonable level of public content and tranquillity rather than an unattainable abstract harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of confusing factional clamor with genuine popular voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Cunning men...raise objections from the difficulty under which the sovereign labors, to distinguish the genuine voice and sentiments of his people, from the clamor of a faction, by which it is so easily counterfeited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While popular sentiment matters, rulers must be cautious in distinguishing transient factional noise from the real disposition of the people; balance and judgment are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration must be unified—avoid 'double cabinet' divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: That form...which brings the whole body of government into confusion and contempt...the invention of the double cabinet...attend very little to [the outward ministers'] remonstrances...these shadows of ministers have nothing to do in the ultimate disposal of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A divided internal administration (an 'interior cabinet' separate from outward administration) produces contradiction, impotence abroad and at home, lost credibility, and foreign contempt; coherent unified councils are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent, persevering policy towards dependencies and foreign affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: They are convinced by sufficient experience, that no plan, either of lenity, or rigor, can be pursued with uniformity and perseverance...They look to themselves...They grow every day into alienation from this country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inconsistent, vacillating administration alienates colonies/dependencies; coherent, steady policy and uniform administration are necessary to retain their confidence and interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dependence on military force for civil governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Fierce licentiousness begets violent restraints. The military arm is the sole reliance; and then...it is the sword that governs. The civil power...perishes by the assistance it receives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on military force to control domestic disorder corrodes civil authority and constitutional government; the law and civil institutions must retain primacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not foster or patronize organized disorder (hired mobs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unable to rule the multitude, they endeavour to raise divisions amongst them. One mob is hired to destroy another...Men become pensioners of state on account of their abilities in the array of riot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using or rewarding agents of disorder as a political expedient increases licentiousness and public discontent, creating durable problems and undermining legitimate authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid system of favoritism that impoverishes and degrades the sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: This system of favoritism...has sunk [the king] into a state of unnatural poverty...tarnished the splendor of his court, sunk his dignity, galled his feelings, discomposed the whole order and happiness of his private life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favours and patronage that concentrate advantage in court factions can both waste public resources and degrade the sovereign’s dignity and private happiness; rule of interest, not public good, tends to prevail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers should be acceptable to the people; the crown should not reward unpopularity
rubrics_metrics.description: There is something very courtly in this. But it is a principle pregnant with all sorts of mischief...to say that 'That the king has thought proper to appoint them' is sufficient reason for supporting ministers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appointments made solely because the sovereign selects them, without regard to public acceptability, turn ambition away from public virtues and toward courtly favour; popular approbation should matter in appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: The House of Commons must reflect the feelings of the nation
rubrics_metrics.description: The virtue, spirit, and essence of a House of Commons consists in its being the express image of the feelings of the nation...It was designed as a control for the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commons should bear the stamp of the actual disposition of the people; if it is wholly untouched by public opinion it ceases to fulfil its representative character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commons’ proper functions: vigilance, financial oversight, openness to complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: A vigilant and jealous eye over executory and judicial magistracy; an anxious care of public money; an openness, approaching towards facility, to public complaint: these seem to be the true characteristics of a House of Commons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than becoming part of standing government, the Commons should exercise oversight of executive/judicial officers, guard public finances, and be accessible to popular grievance—acting as a control for the people.
